posts.post_subject: Muse with me, o intrepid holographers, on multiple exposures
posts.content_md:
Hello All!

I am back once again with copious quantities of gibberish, and would this time love to hear what folks think on the matter of exposing more than one image into a single plate. I find myself wondering - and unable to experiment at this time - about just exactly this phenomenon occurs...

I have only ever attempted single exposures. but multiples... I understand this to be possible with a change (maybe only slight) in reference angle... I personally work with VRP-M and have found success in total energy densities (reflection) of 75 µjoules/cm². When all is said and done, the plate will darken rather dark, take a moment or two to bleach, and dry into a reflection hologram. Now... when I picture exposing the plate once to 75 µjoules/cm², jogging my ref beam mirror to the side a touch for a slightly different angle, then exposing again for 75 µjoules/cm², What I envision in the end is a woefully overexposed plate - granted - even if the fringes are cut at different angles, and perhaps even in different locations (maybe mingling with/between first ones), it's still a plate that's recieved way more energy than what is optimal, yes?

Oh and on a related tangent - how about emulsion swell between exposures? I have loose plans to attempt multi-exposure with varying levels of pre-swell between shots (when I'm up and running again), and wonder - does the difference in emulsion thickness alter the index of refraction maybe, and could I then use the same camera geometry for the different (color) exposures? My hope is that I can find a way to copy several different H1 images into a single H2 at the same reference angle, in the spirit of being able to view the final hologram without any ducking, bobbing or weaving.

Aside from the different colors that will be involved per changes in emulsion thickness between exposures, I also understand that just about any pre-exposure bath will wash out preservatives and resultantly make the film all touchy and sensitive - I can grok in fullness the concept of shortening exposure times for these reasons

 - BUT - 

Have no idea how to expose multiple images into a plate without overexposing it in the end or only exposing individual images with a fraction of the energy necessary for a bright image... Won't partial exposures that add up to 75 µjoules/cm² result only in several dim images?

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.post_subject: Muse with me, o intrepid holographers, on multiple exposures
posts.content_md:
I will address the question of psuedocolor as addressing all of your questions would take a book like Graham Saxby's.

You can expose, pre-swell, expose, pre-swell and expose to add red, green and blue to a hologram. I find I have to expose in that order (not blue first) and I have to use about 1/2 of my exposure time for each of the three colors. (This has to be adjusted for each hologram). You can change the objects between each exposure and end up with three different colored objects in the same hologram.

Here is an interesting reference from the wiki:

[http://www.holographyforum.org/HoloWiki ... nolimining](http://www.holographyforum.org/HoloWiki/index.php/Triethanolimining)

*grins* I guess I did go a bit overboard there...

But yah - you nailed it - that's exactly what I'm going for - Three different objects in three different colors.. And I presume there is no magic bullet solution for the matter of exposure times.. Just have to figure that out for myself 

But seriously... You got results from expose, swell, expose, swell? I tried things in that order myself (as it all seemed much easier that way), but it didn't work (presumably for a variety of reasons) and I later read that the "preferred" order of operation is swell, expose, swell, expose. Mother of.... That's a lot of work! Is OK. I don't mind (and have nothing better to do) - and at least it levels the playing field as far bromide removal across the board....

Dig and dug. I'll just have to play some. Will someone please at least tell me - when I go to finally develop this multiexposed plate, it's gonna go DARK QUICK, isn't it? Or is it?

posts.topic_title: Muse with me, o intrepid holographers, on multiple exposures
posts.author: john kaufman
posts.post_subject: Muse with me, o intrepid holographers, on multiple exposures
posts.content_md:
Yes, Justin, you will end up with a very heavily exposed plate with multiple exposures. In the olden days, 10-25 years ago, I used nearly full exposure time for each exposure (this was with Agfa plates). Development density was the same as for a fully exposed single exposure. Beam ratios were very close.

I used a different exposure scheme from Colin. I started with blue and worked to red. The pre-sensitizing from the trieth. was more consistent if I worked that way. If you do red first, the plate should at least start in a water bath for a little bit of presensitization.

You will need to plan your final image with great care so that you can control hot spots. Control of the shape and position of the reference beam on the H1 and H2 are also important to reducing information to be recorded, and in determining color playback position in the final image.

I would suggest being able to make a killer bright and clean one color before moving on to multiple exposures.

Some thought into the final hologram - This is a new concept to me as I now finally realize that holograms of a single something are boring - building scenes - yeauh. In theory, with the addition of collimated reference and H1 replay beams in my setup will put me in a position to work with real images that will follow the rules! ie, land where I expect them to, remain in focus, etc...

posts.topic_title: Muse with me, o intrepid holographers, on multiple exposures
posts.author: john kaufman
posts.post_subject: Muse with me, o intrepid holographers, on multiple exposures
posts.content_md:
Justin, usually one does vary the reference angle of the H2 so that the colors play back together. Jeff Blyth, when he first described pre-swelling color control in the late 70's, kept the angle the same and the images did not play back together. Whatever works for your final image. See if you can find the papers that Steve McGrew, Lon Moore, and I presented in 1982 at the Lake Forest/SPIE symposium. They cover most of the basics.

Note that Lon got his colors to play back together by selectively lighting only parts of his H1 (his H1 was large enough so that he could light the top, middle, and bottom of the plate with a wide and narrow reference beam). His two or three exposures played back with three views of the object overlapping in one spot. This is a good technique when registration is not so important.

I usually controled color play back by varying the H2 reference. Remember that even when a single H1 is used, and the colors play back together, they will be in register only at the film plane. You have to plan the final image to minimize the visual effect of colors that play back together but lose their registration.

I also did a lot of work with multi-color shadowgrams. They could be very bright with the right diffuser and the color mixing effects were very satisfying. I chose to vary the reference angles but one could use Lon's techinque and light parts of the diffuser so that it would play back in the same position without moving your reference beam.
